parts.note: Count Dracula turns into a bat, so he is a man who is also a bat, read as a two-word description

explanation.surface: A one-word question about the famous vampire.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark tells you the name is to be read literally: Dracula is a man who becomes a bat.
explanation.definitionFit: The vampire count shape-shifts into a flying mammal, so he is literally a human who is also that creature.

clue.text: The instrument of public opinion polls ?

definitions.text: The instrument of public opinion polls ?

parts.words: The instrument of public opinion polls
parts.note: read as an instrument that measures the pressure of public opinion, as a weather gauge measures air pressure

explanation.surface: What tool do pollsters use to gauge the public mood?
explanation.walkthrough: The weather instrument that measures atmospheric pressure is used figuratively for any indicator of the public mood, such as a poll.
explanation.definitionFit: A gauge of air pressure is commonly used as a figure for any sensitive indicator of changing public feeling.

clue.text: Archer et fils in Dickens's bank

parts.note: William Tell, the legendary Swiss archer
fils is French for son

explanation.surface: A family firm, Archer and Son, named as the bank in a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Archer et fils' looks like a French firm's name; Tell is the famous archer and 'fils' is French for son. Tellson's is the London bank in A Tale of Two Cities.
explanation.definitionFit: Tellson's is the old London banking house where Mr Lorry works in A Tale of Two Cities.

parts.note: the first woman, tempted with the forbidden fruit in Eden, is seen as a female fruit-seller of a sort

explanation.surface: A one-word question about the first woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark asks for a playful description: Eve in Eden is the woman associated with the forbidden fruit, traditionally an apple.
explanation.definitionFit: A female fruit-seller dealing in pippins is a playful title for the first woman, who handed Adam the forbidden fruit.

clue.text: With which I celebrate top academician

definitions.text: With which I celebrate top academician

parts.note: PRA stands for President of the Royal Academy, the most senior British academician
to sing of something is to celebrate it in song

explanation.surface: Someone describes the words they use to honour the head of the Royal Academy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: PRA (President of the Royal Academy) followed by I SING; and laudatory words are what one celebrates a great man with.
explanation.definitionFit: Laudatory words are the means by which a speaker extols or honours someone such as an eminent academician.

annotationWithheld.why: Dud tanner not wanted: DUD TANNER is an anagram of the answer but no separate word signals it; 'Dud' would be fodder and anagram indicator at once

clue.text: It may be news, but the printer gives it little space

parts.note: an em is a printer's unit of space, the width of the letter M

explanation.surface: A news story that the typesetter squeezes into a tiny gap.
explanation.walkthrough: An em is a printer's measure of space; 'the printer gives it little space' tells you to add EM to IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A single piece of news in a paper is called by the same word as a single article on a list.

annotationWithheld.why: Life, man, should excite: LIFE MAN is an anagram of the answer but no clue word signals the anagram, so the fodder would have to act as its own indicator

parts.note: gas is idle talk, empty words
a PS, postscript, is words added after a letter is finished

explanation.surface: Someone runs on talking until they are out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: GAS is empty talk and PS (postscript) is more words added at the end; 'and then' places one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp intakes of breath, as in shock or exhaustion, are sudden catchings of breath.

parts.note: one of the four March sisters in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women, the gentle one who dies young

explanation.surface: A girl born in March, or a girl who marches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like the month, but it is the family name of the sisters Meg, Jo, Amy and the fourth in Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: The shy third sister in Alcott's Little Women belongs to the March family.

parts.note: a recidivist is a habitual offender, and his going back to crime is a falling back into old ways

explanation.surface: A habitual criminal comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' suggests a homecoming from prison, but it means the return to crime, the backsliding that defines a recidivist.
explanation.definitionFit: Falling back into a former bad habit, especially offending again, is exactly what marks out a repeat offender.

parts.note: the most famous French legal case of the 1890s, the end of the century, was the treason affair of the Jewish army captain Alfred

explanation.surface: A celebrated court case in France at the close of the nineteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: Fin de siècle, French for 'end of the century', places the case in the 1890s, when an army captain was wrongly convicted of treason.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Alfred's wrongful treason conviction became the great political scandal of 1890s France, known simply as the Affair.

clue.text: Employer and employed supplying a touch of expertise ?

parts.note: a master is one who employs servants or workmen
a hand is an employed worker, as on a farm or ship

explanation.surface: Boss and worker together lend a skilled touch to a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employer and employed' sounds like labour relations, but the two words simply supply the two halves of the answer in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A master-hand is a skilled practitioner or the expert skill itself, the touch of someone thoroughly proficient.

clue.text: " In thy possession lies A unparalleled " (A. & C)

definitions.text: In thy possession lies A unparalleled

parts.words: In thy possession lies A unparalleled
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra, where Charmian speaks over the dead queen of a girl without equal

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with a word missing, credited to Antony and Cleopatra.
explanation.walkthrough: A. & C. is Antony and Cleopatra; Charmian's words over Cleopatra's body are 'A ___ unparallel'd', so the blank is a word for a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: In the play the dead queen is called a girl without equal, using the Scots and poetic word for a young woman.

clue.text: Instrument of support for agricultural machinery

parts.note: pro means in support of, in favour
a tractor is the farm vehicle that pulls ploughs and other machinery

explanation.surface: A gadget that backs up farm equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument' is a geometry instrument here, the one for measuring angles; PRO (for, in support) comes before TRACTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A semicircular drawing instrument for measuring angles is a standard item in a geometry set.

annotationWithheld.why: No rest for these muscles: NO REST is an anagram of the answer but no clue word signals the anagram, so 'No rest' would be fodder and indicator at once

parts.note: a student of correct writing is charmed by the ways words are written, and 'spell' also means a charm

explanation.surface: The magic charms worked by an expert in correct writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enchantments' plays on 'spell' as a charm: an orthographist's spells are the forms in which words are written.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert in orthography deals with the written forms of words, punningly the spells of a magic charm.

clue.text: Words without song would be so stuffy. !

definitions.meaning: lyrics without a tune, an air, are literally lacking an air
a stuffy room is short of fresh air

explanation.surface: Lyrics with no melody would be dull and stuffy.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes 'air' in its musical sense, a tune; the second in its everyday sense of breathable atmosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking a tune and lacking ventilation are both described by the same adjective built on the word for melody and atmosphere.

annotationWithheld.why: Sees right through a rubberneck: SEES RIGHT is an anagram of the answer but no clue word fairly signals it ('through' is not an anagram indicator), so the fodder would be its own indicator

parts.note: rodents proverbially desert a sinking ship, so a contest among them is a scramble of rodents

explanation.surface: Who will be first off the doomed vessel?
explanation.walkthrough: Rats are said to desert a sinking ship; the phrase for a fierce, pointless competitive struggle is read literally as a contest among those rodents.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a cut-throat competitive scramble, especially for career success, literally names a contest between rodents.

clue.text: Needlewoman's equipment that takes some beating

definitions.meaning: an embroidery frame of two hoops holding the fabric taut
a drum, an instrument that is beaten

explanation.surface: Sewing gear that is hard to better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes some beating' means hard to surpass, but here it is literal: the word also names a drum.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names a circular embroidery frame and a drum, the frame taking its name from its drum-like shape.

definitions.meaning: giving a title or name to something
a small bird such as the meadow pipit, an old name for a little songbird

explanation.surface: Putting a name to a small bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface links the two halves, but they are separate senses: the act of giving a title, and an old name for the pipit or other small bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving something a title is one sense; the other is a dialect name for a small bird such as the pipit or titmouse.

clue.text: Beginning of an idea among the tinkling cymbals

indicators.note: the answer lies among the letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A new thought starts amid the ringing of cymbals, a nod to 1 Corinthians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Among' tells you the answer sits inside 'tinkling'; 'tinkling cymbals' echoes 1 Corinthians 13.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint first notion or slight suspicion of something is a hint or glimmer of an idea.

clue.text: Unchanged though knobs are sometimes added

definitions.meaning: the British retort 'the ___ to you, with knobs on' returns an insult with embellishment

explanation.surface: Something stays as it was, though decorations get attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The same to you with knobs on' is a British playground retort, throwing an insult back with extra force.
explanation.definitionFit: Unaltered means identical; and the jeering British reply 'the same to you with knobs on' adds the knobs.

clue.text: " How pleasant to know Mr. Lear ! Who has written such volumes of" (Lear)

definitions.text: How pleasant to know Mr. Lear ! Who has written such volumes of

parts.words: How pleasant to know Mr. Lear ! Who has written such volumes of
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Edward Lear's own self-portrait poem, where he says he has written volumes of nonsense

explanation.surface: A line of Edward Lear's comic verse about himself with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's poem runs 'How pleasant to know Mr. Lear! / Who has written such volumes of ___!', the missing word meaning nonsense or rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem Lear modestly calls his writing a mass of nonsense, using the everyday word for rubbish or material.

clue.text: Sailor comes by B.E.A. jet with luck!

indicators.note: the answer comes by, that is is obtained from, these letters once they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor gets a lucky flight on a British European Airways jet.
explanation.walkthrough: B.E.A. was British European Airways. 'Comes by' signals that the letters of BEA JET and LUCK are rearranged to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluejacket is a seaman of the navy, named for the blue jacket of the uniform.

indicators.note: the word sits inside the name for Greece that follows

explanation.surface: Rossini's Italian Girl turns up in Greece rather than Algiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts the answer inside 'Hellas', the Greek name for Greece. The surface echoes Rossini's opera The Italian Girl in Algiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ella is the old literary Italian pronoun for 'she', the word an Italian uses for a girl just mentioned; it is also a girl's name.

explanation.surface: Dependable business associates.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as one phrase but are separate: an adjective meaning steady, and a noun for a business partnership.
explanation.definitionFit: Unyielding and steady is one sense; a business run by partners is the other.

parts.note: read as More-land, the imaginary ideal island described by Sir Thomas More in his 1516 book

explanation.surface: Something that tastes of a place called Moreland.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Moreland' as More-land: Sir Thomas More's land is his ideal commonwealth, so having its flavour means being idealistic.
explanation.definitionFit: Idealistic and impossibly perfect, like the imagined island commonwealth of Sir Thomas More's famous book.

clue.text: Kind of window the French put round the top storey

indicators.note: the French article is put round the room so it encloses it

parts.note: le is the French masculine word for 'the'
an attic is the room or storey just under the roof

explanation.surface: A French householder fits a special window around the attic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put round' makes LE enclose ATTIC: L(ATTIC)E.
explanation.definitionFit: A lattice window has small panes set in a diagonal criss-cross framework of lead or wood.

clue.text: Doctor deep in the wood takes the lead

indicators.note: the doctor sits deep within the wood, so one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: a forest is a large wood
MO is a medical officer, an army doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor lost in a forest steps out in front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deep in' puts MO inside FOREST: FORE(MO)ST. The definition is 'the lead', the position of being first, with 'takes' joining.
explanation.definitionFit: Being first in position or rank is being in the lead, ahead of all others.

parts.note: Oom Paul, Afrikaans (of Dutch descent) for Uncle Paul, was the nickname of the Boer president of the Transvaal

explanation.surface: An exclamation about an elderly Dutch relative.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Dutch uncle' is a stern adviser, but here it is Paul, president of the Transvaal, known to the Boers as 'Oom Paul', Uncle Paul.
explanation.definitionFit: The Transvaal's Boer president Paul was nicknamed Oom Paul, Afrikaans for Uncle Paul.
